title: Optimal query cost of reducing testing adaptivity
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors over all integers \(q,k\ge1\) and \(0\le\ell<k\), \[F(q,k,\ell)=\sup\{q_\ell(n,\mathcal P,\varepsilon):n\ge1,\ \varnothing\ne\mathcal P\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,\ 0<\varepsilon\le1,\ q_k(n,\mathcal P,\varepsilon)\le q\},\] the worst query cost of reducing a Boolean property tester from \(k+1\) batches to \(\ell+1\) batches.
why: Quantifies the general price of replacing sequential information gathering by fewer batches. A substantive universal bound would apply across Boolean property testing, beyond the behavior of one particular property.

importance.reason: A general resource tradeoff for adaptive Boolean property testing; a precise quantitative target is needed to distinguish a substantive advance from the existing simulations. Existing score retained.

sentences: A property tester probes bits in batches and may choose later batches using previous answers.
The source counts one more batch than the number of adaptive rounds.
The target is the largest query budget needed after reducing the number of rounds, among properties testable with the original budget.
Both the property and its proximity and error guarantees remain fixed during the reduction.
The benchmark asks for matching bounds with constants independent of all three resource parameters.

definitions: An input \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) is available through queries to individual coordinates. Its distance to the known property \(\mathcal P\) is \(n^{-1}\min_{y\in\mathcal P}|\{i:x_i\ne y_i\}|\). A tester accepts every member with probability at least \(2/3\) and rejects every input at distance strictly greater than \(\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(2/3\); other inputs have no correctness requirement. Under the source convention, \(j\) rounds of adaptivity mean \(j+1\) batches \(Q_0,\ldots,Q_j\). All coordinates in one batch are chosen before their answers are revealed. The coordinates and size of every later batch may depend on all earlier answers; empty batches are permitted. A randomized tester is a finite probability distribution over deterministic batch-query trees, each of which returns a bit on every input. Probabilities may be arbitrary real numbers; this is the nonuniform query-complexity model, without a computational or randomness-generation cost. Each selected tree’s total queries are bounded on every input, and cost is their worst case over the support and inputs. Let \(q_j(n,\mathcal P,\varepsilon)\) be the least such bound among all valid testers. Reading every coordinate shows \(q_j\le n\). The tester may depend arbitrarily on the fixed property, length and proximity parameter; no uniform synthesis from a property description is requested. Querying a coordinate already read gives no additional information and can be omitted. The same property, distance and error convention occur on both sides of \(F\). The source’s complete nonadaptive simulation shows \(F(q,k,\ell)\le2^q-1\), so the supremum is finite; since all values are integers, it is a maximum. The desired precision is a positive function \(g(q,k,\ell)\) and one absolute \(C\ge1\) with \(C^{-1}g\le F\le Cg\) for every admissible triple. The comparison constant must not depend on a parameter or on a hidden property.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous positive comparison function and a Lean proof of both universal constant-factor bounds on the full parameter domain. The upper bound must cover adaptive batch sizes, and the lower bound must be witnessed by permitted properties and proximity parameters. A bound only for deleting one round, fixed-size batches or a selected regime does not determine this tradeoff. Numerical 0.01 error is not the precision for this asymptotic-complexity target.

context_blocks.text: The source asks how query complexity changes when a tester may use fewer adaptive batches. Its general question does not prescribe a particular exponent improvement.

The authorized editorial completion defines the extremal simulation cost and asks for matching constant-factor bounds. This is a quantitative development of the broader upper-bound question, not a claim that the source already asks for matching lower bounds.
The source already proves a one-round reduction bound and stresses that later batch sizes may depend on previous answers.
